October housing starts jump led by a surge in multifamily, but permits, a leading indicator, fell to the lowest since May 2020, with single-family permits falling the most since February 2021.

▪️ Housing starts jumped 9.9% to 1.309 million, the biggest gain since June, well above the 1.250 million consensus (Morgan Stanley’s 1.320 million was closest), though both September and August were revised down, September to 1.191 million from 1.221 million.
▪️ Most of the gain was multifamily, up 25.5% to 433,000, while single-family rose 4.0% to 864,000 after September was revised down to 831,000, the lowest since March 2023.
▪️ Building permits fell 7.4% to 1.295 million, the lowest since May 2020, well below the 1.377 million consensus.
▪️ Single-family permits fell 8.7%, the most since February 2021, to 772,000, the lowest since January 2023, down in all four regions (West -14.5%, the most since April 2020); the three-month average is the lowest since March 2023.
▪️ Completions rose 6.5% to 1.272 million, while units under construction edged down to 1.272 million, 442,000 below the October 2022 record.
▪️ The backdrop: NAHB builder sentiment fell to 25 in November, the lowest since April 2012, and Freddie Mac’s 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.33% in October, the highest monthly average since November 2023.

@C_Barraud’s Wednesday Morning Brief contained an interesting post from @sentimentrader that fits with the outperformance of the S&P 500 vs the Nasdaq-100: while over half the Nasdaq 100 is in a bear market (54% of its stocks are down 20%+ from their 52-week highs), just 32% of the S&P 500 is. The 20-day average of that gap just crossed 18.5 percentage points. After past crossings, the S&P 500 was higher three months later only 3 of 10 times, averaging a 2.9% loss.

But as SentimenTrader notes, half of those signals came in 2000–02. So I rebuilt the gap from 2011 using The Trading Tools’ free breadth data (which is the history of the free data - a great resource).

▪️ The gap is now the widest since 2011. Its 20-day average hit 19.9 points Tuesday, above the 2022 tech-bear peak (16.9) and the 2012 peak (17.1). It widened again Tuesday to 60% vs. 35.7%.

▪️ The 18.5 line has been crossed only one other time since 2011, also this year, in August. After the August crossing, the S&P 500 was down 2.3% three months later and the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) was down 5.4%.

▪️ But lowering the bar to the widest 5% of readings (13.6 points), with each episode dated to its first close above that level, gives five finished signals: November 2012 (S&P 500 +6.7% three months later), March 2021 (+8.0%), January 2022 (−7.9%), February 2026 (+6.9%) and July 2026 (+4.7%).

▪️ So that’s 4 of 5 higher, averaging +3.7%, vs. +3.1% for all days since 2011.

The one loser, then, was January 2022, the start of that year’s tech bear market. Combine that with SentimenTrader’s history, where half the signals (and most of the damage) came in 2000–02, and the pattern seems to be that the gap has been a warning, but outside of tech busts it has been a buying opportunity.

In that regard, SentimenTrader notes the gap closes one of two ways: the Nasdaq recovers, or more S&P 500 stocks fall into bear markets. In all four good episodes, the Nasdaq’s bear-market share was lower three months later (sharply in 2012, 29% to 17%, and 2021, 18% to 10%; modestly in both 2026 episodes). In contrast, in 2022 the Nasdaq’s share climbed from 39% to 62%, and the S&P 500’s more than doubled, peaking at 47%.

Right now the Nasdaq’s share is still rising (46% at the August signal, 60% now), which signals continued caution.

It’s a small sample and not SentimenTrader’s exact signal, so treat it as context rather than a timing tool.

Many retail and enterprise FLOP miners to be ask us:
- What's the best hardware?
- How do I setup my hardware to optimise performance?

We cannot answer those questions. We can tell you the block reward, and that it's weighted by amount of inference processed measured by floating point operations (compute) meaning if in one block your miner processed 100 gigaflops out of a total of 200 gigaflops, you earn half of the miner block reward.

If you buy hardware that can serve a certain AI model, and that model is not in demand, you will process zero inference requests and earn nothing.

If you want to better forecast the types of models most in demand for agentic work, look at the most popular models on Open Router for example.

Worst case, try out your configuration, and adjust your setup based on actual results.

- What's the best hardware?
- How do I setup my hardware to optimise performance?

We cannot answer those questions. We can tell you the block reward, and that it's weighted by amount of inference processed measured by floating point operations (compute) meaning if in one block your miner processed 100 gigaflops out of a total of 200 gigaflops, you earn half of the miner block reward.

If you buy hardware that can serve a certain AI model, and that model is not in demand, you will process zero inference requests and earn nothing.

If you want to better forecast the types of models most in demand for agentic work, look at the most popular models on Open Router for example.

Worst case, try out your configuration, and adjust your setup based on actual results.

The Fed hiked for two years, and the private sector barely felt it. Washington felt all of it.

Corporate America and homeowners locked in record-low rates during the pandemic, so corporate interest costs as a share of GDP actually fell while rates rose. The federal interest bill went the other way, more than doubling from about $500 billion in 2020 to roughly $1.25 trillion today.

The cost of higher rates landed on the government, not companies or consumers. That is why tightening barely dented the economy, and why the debt is the real pressure point. Every rate the Fed holds high, the Treasury pays for.

here's every skill crypto forces you to learn, if you stay long enough:

1: position sizing
 you size by what you can afford to lose. you learn how to take bets and when to take them.

2: taking profit
 you learn to sell into strength. gains you never took don't pay rent.

3: macro
 you learn what CPI, PPI and the FOMC do to your bags. i've watched every FOMC meeting since 2022 because one decision can move everything i hold.

4: tokenomics
 this has carry over, you understand finance at a level most people never reach, you can read unlocks, emissions and supply.

5: narratives
 you learn to tell a narrative with users and money behind it from one that's just a marketing stunt.

6: crowd behaviour
 euphoria at the top, silence at the bottom. the same people are loudest both times.
you can spot changes societal shifts and hysteria. 

7: security and sovereignty
 crypto lets you hold money no bank or government can freeze. that only works if you hold your own keys. so you learn self-custody, keep your seed phrase offline and check every transaction before you sign. being your own bank means nobody can reverse a mistake for you.
it teaches you ultimate diligence.

8: on-chain research
 following wallets, checking contracts and seeing where the money actually goes.
you’re able to conduct deep research and investigations.

9: your own psychology
 FOMO after a green candle. revenge trades after a red one. you learn your triggers or they run your account.
you understand your psyche better than people who’ve spent thousands on therapy.

10: survival
 keeping enough on the side to live through a bear market. the next cycle only pays the people with chips.

11: adaptability
 dropping a thesis the moment the data changes. the market doesn't care what you believed yesterday.

12: networking
 the best information comes from people you've built trust with over years.
anyone calling it luck has never paid for these lessons.

and there's one skill that ties all 12 together: game theory.

every trade has someone on the other side, and each skill on this list really asks what that person will do next.

tokenomics: what do insiders do the day their tokens unlock?

narratives: who's pushing this, and when do they need someone to sell to?

crowd behaviour: what does everyone do at the top, and what will you do?

macro: how will the market react to the fed, on top of what the fed actually says?

networking: what does someone gain by sharing this with you?

once you start asking what everyone else wants and what they'll do to get it, you see it everywhere. crypto, business, negotiations, your career.

that's why i think it's the most valuable skill on earth, and crypto teaches it faster than anything else.

anyone calling it luck or a waste of time is to much of a mouth breather to look at the bigger picture.

Honest take on the AI Nuremberg trailer from someone who has been pretty resistant to AI film

The Good:
+ Amazing imagery, worldbuilding and translation of the lore, if you know it
+ Insane 1 person can do this and the visual/audio editing makes me hyped for the film, first time feeling that
+ Huge reduction in cost compared to previous tech (CGI etc) to render and create entire new worlds, even if all film doesn't go this way, a new industry will be born around it
+ the marvel/netflix-ification of cinema means we've already got a ton of human made slop that is no better than this now. So complaints purely directed at it being derivative fall flat
+ This still needed someone who knew the lore, picked the shots and timed the edit. That's the impressive part
+ Overall insane how far we've come from Will Smith eating spaghetti

The Less Good/Skeptical:
- A lot of what makes it work is lifted from recent films (1917 visual, boots from 28 years later) which is closer to a collage than inspiring something new. Whether AI can ever truly do that is another question*
- It's a trailer. Mapping that out into a film that not only makes sense but is engaging is infinitely harder and a different skillset
- Most complaints about AI content are dialogue and characters. It's hard to judge that as there is none of that here. Ultimately it's what films live or die on

Overall I'm super impressed. Especially given the speed of the improvement in AI, but it's worth pointing out that is all it is for now - a trailer, and the parts missing are exactly where AI has been weakest so far

I will see it if it's made. Out of sheer curiosity if nothing else. Which says a lot about how far it's come

Good corporate governance should be defined as founder control, with dual class stock, not board control. The board is just an advisory board. The shareholder vote is a backup in the event of issues, and shareholder sales are the extreme backup.

This should be obvious from the financial performance of founder-led global tech companies vs manager-led incumbents. And also obvious in terms of just how much value these boards typically consume rather than produce.

After all, typical board members aren’t like execs that a CEO can actually assign tasks. Instead, they have power, and often time to scheme amongst themselves, but lack true operating knowledge of the underlying company. The exception is when there are real founders on the board themselves — but those are exceptions.

To be clear, the 20th century MBA-style corporate governance playbook was actually fine for the era of General Mills, General Motors, and General Electric. In that time period, the individual didn’t matter that much. They didn’t have the leverage that computers give them.

But now the Internet has obsolesced all that. So YC, Founders Fund, and a16z are much better business schools than Harvard Business School, which is culturally obsolete because it is technologically obsolete. The world it was implicitly premised on no longer exists.

However, all these intuitions and best practices, the conventions that built billion and trillion dollar companies, have only been informally advocated in blog posts and contracts. To change the defaults, we’ll need to actually write a new curriculum.

The frustrating part about the stablecoin drain is that the fix already exists.

Since 2022 stablecoin supply has moved inversely with T-bill yields (-0.62 correlation on 90-day changes). Rates aren't the only driver, but when bills pay more, stablecoins lose out because holders earn nothing.

Tokenised money market funds hold the same T-bills, pay you the yield & live onchain. In principle that makes them a better product than a stablecoin, and better than a traditional money fund too, as they can settle and be posted as collateral 24/7.

In TradFi, money funds grow when rates are high or markets are stressed, as people park cash. Onchain, they should be the offset when stablecoins shrink, but at $17.1B they're only 6% of stablecoin supply. Many of the big ones are for wealthy investors only (BlackRock's needs $5M, JPMorgan's $1M), and even the retail ones need ID checks, approved wallets and business-day redemptions.

Fix that and I expect this becomes one of the biggest growth areas onchain.

There’s a lot of talk about agents replacing apps. I think the more interesting future is how they work together.

Word, Excel and PowerPoint are now part of the Copilot experience. And Copilot is becoming part of the apps people have loved and used for decades.

That matters because people have years of muscle memory in these tools. They know how to adjust a spreadsheet, refine a slide, edit a document. That familiarity is an enormous asset to build on.

An agent can do the research, build the model and draft the presentation. You can jump into Excel to check an assumption or PowerPoint to make the story yours, then hand the work back to the agent. Moving between delegation and doing should feel natural.

For agents to become part of everyday work, they need to meet people where they are and work with what they already know.

Apps and agents form an ecosystem. Each makes the other more useful. The agent moves the work forward, and the familiar tools let you shape the result.
